t: Character-SwitchingI & The Pursuit of the Poised Life
q: If we’re to reach our potential, we must pursue the integrated life; we must strive toward being one-faced. Our aim is to be like those integers we learn about in math class: whole numbers, devoid of cunning; what you see is what you get.

Most people think of poise as calm, self-assured dignity; but I call it “just being you.” When we have poise, we’re not acting, faking or pretending. We’re not trying to be something we’re not, nor are we attempting to live up to others’ expectations. Therefore, when we are being who we really are, we’ll have a greater likelihood of functioning nearer our own level of competency.

Of course we’d dress up for the Governor’s Ball. Of course I wear slacks and a tie when I teach and sweatpants if I’m home with my children. The problem isn’t when we code-switch, but when we character-switch.
If one period I’m teaching students I supposedly care about and the next period I’m gossiping about them with other teachers, that’s character-switching.
You don’t go out and decide that you’ll be someone with integrity issues, someone blind to the reality that everyone else sees. You slip into the disintegrated life, the many selves, bit by bit.
First, accept that you struggle here. Second, analyze the problem and relentlessly pursue it’s solution.
When we allow tiny instances of character-switching, they act like cracks in a sidewalk, worsening over time if left unaddressed.
x: Stuart argues that pursuing an integrated, one-faced life is strategic, not merely moral, because it stops energy being wasted on playing different selves.
Drawing on John Wooden's idea of poise in the Pyramid of Success, he defines poise as simply being yourself and so functioning nearer your true ability.
He distinguishes harmless code-switching, adjusting dress and register to context, from character-switching, such as caring for students in one period and gossiping about them in the next.

t: How To Build Deep Trust With Your New Class https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2016/08/27/how-to-build-deep-trust-with-your-new-class/
q: It’s important because when your students trust you—really trust you— everything is easier.
Somewhere in the back of their mind, perhaps just outside of conscious awareness, they believe that telling little white lies here and there can’t hurt.
Because every time you play loose with the truth, every time you say one thing and do another, your students take notice. And it changes them.
Building deep and abiding trust, of the kind that inspires an almost reverent-like respect, is nothing more than following through on your promises and being truthful with your words.
Being a teacher of integrity doesn’t take great skill or effort. You don’t have to look or dress a certain way.
So make it a point this school year to do exactly what you say. Be real and transparent, a straight shooter , consistent in word and action.
x: Trust is foundational: when students trust a teacher, virtually every area of classroom management gets easier.
He observes that teachers who consider themselves fully honest with adults often tell small "white lies" to students, over-praising undeserved work or overlooking misbehavior to avoid a hassle.
Students notice inconsistency between what a teacher says and does, and respond with reduced motivation and respect.
Building deep trust, he says, requires nothing more than consistently following through on promises and being truthful, not perfection.

Linsin argues that trust is an overlooked but critical foundation of classroom management: when students genuinely trust a teacher, every other area of management becomes easier, and when they don't, nothing works as it should.
He closes by urging teachers to be a genuine "straight shooter" from the first week of school onward.

t: How To Handle A Class That Tests You Right From The Get-Go rom-the-get-go/
q: It’s disheartening—and only natural to feel as if you did something wrong.
So if it happens to you, there is no need to panic. In fact, your first response should be to do absolutely nothing.
Just wait. Breathe. Observe. Smile inwardly—because you’re going to fix it.
Most teachers will try to enforce consequences as fast as they can, but this is a mistake with a large group of misbehaving students because it risks inciting aggressive and disrespectful pushback.

Exceptional classroom management, especially with a tough class, takes courage . And if you’re not feeling confident, if your heart is beating out of your chest and your palms are sweaty, then fake it .
Teach it until they “get it.” Teach it until they know that rebelling is futile.
x: Linsin describes the disheartening scenario of a class that begins misbehaving almost immediately after the teacher introduces a classroom management plan, and reassures teachers this doesn't doom the year.
His prescribed first response is to do nothing: stop, breathe, and observe rather than reacting or rushing to enforce consequences, which can incite pushback.

t: Refutation Two-Chance: A New Frontier for Pop-Up Debate
q: The best pop-up debates I've ever facilitated were at the end of last school year when I applied Les' rigorous Refutation Two-Chance to pop-up debates, and they were the best because they were hard. I knew it was hard because, where my outspoken students typically beg for pop-up debates, after our first Refutation Two-Chance these students were asking, “Can we just do it the old way?

Weeping and gnashing of teeth. Kids were frustrated for a variety of reasons: - First, they weren't used to points in pop-up debates or to the existence of “rounds” or to the general idea of sticking to one argument before moving on to another one. This made the comfortable kids uncomfortable and the kids with a fear of public speaking pretty scared.

Second, by the time they got to the second chance at refutation, most kids in the room had forgotten the counter-argument and the argument. This made refutation really hard. - Solution: Next time, we would all take notes.

Third, I had rarely “judged” their debate performances live before and never with points on the line, and so I was super clunky in working through whether a counter-argument had been adequately refuted or not.
I saw a vast improvement in student participation, student success, and clarity of teaching as demonstrated by student learning (both when they spoke up and in the “flow” notes they took).

Second, every student had to take notes using this flow note-taking document (another of Les' tools with slight modifications by me), and I was modeling how to do that on the projector screen. As I modeled, I encouraged students not to copy me verbatim and to use abbreviations that they could make sense of. Sometimes my modeling required me to ask that a given arguer or counter-arguer clarify her work, and this started to produce clearer initial arguments and counter-arguments as the debate progressed.

I have always said that pop-up debate is simple to a fault, and one of those faults is that the pre-debate teaching and modeling can only go so far in ensuring that every student is tracking and grappling with every argument presented by students.
x: Refutation Two-Chance is a harder variant of pop-up debate suited to students whose argumentative work has plateaued.

t: Why Good Rapport With Students Is A Choice You Make Every Day -you-make-every-day/
q: Because when you dislike or resent any one or more of your students, they’ll know it . It’s something you can’t hide.
So, while the key to building influential rapport is nothing more than being consistently pleasant , it’s only possible if you choose to like your students.

And here’s the amazing thing: Once you commit yourself to liking every student and seeing only the best in them—no matter who they are or what they’ve done in the past—they become not so unlikable after all.
So, practically, on the first day of school and thereafter, make it a point to smile at every student.
It’s available to any teacher who guards their heart and mind against negativity, animosity, and resentment. It’s a choice, not a skill.
x: Linsin argues that good rapport with students isn't a personality trait, a skill, or a matter of spending extra time chatting — it's a daily choice to like every student regardless of their behavior.
Rapport is described as a choice, not an innate skill or a function of extra time spent with students.
Choosing to consistently like every student — including difficult ones — creates a virtuous cycle where they begin liking and trusting the teacher back.
Practical rapport-building starts with smiling at every student and treating them like your best-behaved students from day one.

t: Anti-Teacher Credibility: 10 Great Ways to Become Unbelievable (in a Bad Way)
q: What are the ways in which we might lessen our students' belief in our ability to help them succeed? How might we undermine their perceptions of Trust, Competence, Dynamism, and Immediacy?

Manage your classroom unfairly. The sweet and innocent kids are allowed to misbehave once in awhile, but those rowdy ones, or the ones that really know how to push our buttons — they can't be given an inch! (Trust)

Accept that, sometimes, in-class debates or discussions just get loud and obnoxious and rude, and there's nothing you can do about it. I don't have a snarky way of remarking about this one. Just, the thing is, when we don't manage discussions well, and when we don't teach through the hard parts, I think it gives our kids the impression that the wheels have fallen off. (Competence)

Be nice to your students when they are around, but speak ill of them after class. Again, so easy to do. But I think kids are smart, and they can tell when we don't like them. Also, our brains aren't as good at compartmentalizing as we want to think sometimes — when we speak ill of our kids behind their backs, we are going to have a harder time really connecting with them. (Trust, Immediacy)

Pay no mind to your distracting speaking tics. Alternatively: don't film yourself teaching. Watching myself teach is the most painful way for me to see where I could be speaking better or more clearly. It's the only way to detect my PVLEGS glitches. (Dynamism)

Don't commit to hard-and-fast unit end dates. When we commit to summative assessment dates or due dates, and we share those dates with kids, it shows them that we have a plan and we're going to see it through. An additional benefit here is that setting (and struggling with) unit end dates is the only way we get good at figuring out how long stuff really takes. (Competence)

When students fail, don't reflect about how you could have done things differently. Even if 99% of a student's failure seems to be her fault or her choice or whatever, there's still the 1% that I could have had an impact on. (Trust)
x: Credibility can be diagnosed through four components, Trust, Competence, Dynamism and Immediacy, and each bad habit maps to one or more.

Speaking ill of students after class leaks into how you relate to them in class, damaging trust and connection.

t: How A Back-To-School Promise Can Transform Your Teaching Career m-your-teaching-career/
q: This week’s strategy, which consists of making a simple, two-part promise to your students, is about throwing your hat over the wall.
I promise to follow the classroom management plan exactly as we’ve learned it and every time someone misbehaves.
Furthermore, I promise to never yell, scold, use sarcasm, or in any way treat you with disrespect.
From this moment on, I will follow our classroom management plan to a tee and never, ever treat you with disrespect.
Said with conviction, the moment will mark a seismic shift in how your students view school and their relationship with their new teacher.
With those two remarkably unsettling possibilities thrown out the window—that is, inconsistency and intimidation—the freedom to learn and truly love school is all that remains.
But if you do it, if you’re willing to bet on yourself and your ability to keep your word, your teaching life will never be the same again.
x: The strategy is a scripted "two-part promise" delivered after the full classroom management plan has been taught and modeled.
Part one promises to follow the plan exactly, every time; part two promises never to yell, scold, or disrespect students.

He instructs teachers to deliver each part slowly, let it linger in silence for thirty seconds, and repeat it for emphasis, arguing the ritual marks a seismic shift in how students perceive the teacher and the classroom.
Removing both inconsistency and intimidation from the classroom is what makes students stop testing the teacher.
